rejected.title: Strategies to improve liveability
card: Liveability is how well a place meets the needs of the people who live there. Local councils run many services that shape it.
Public spaces
Parks, playgrounds and town squares give people places to meet, play and relax.
Paths and transport
Walking and cycling paths and bus or train links help people get to work, school and shops.
Waste services
Rubbish collection and recycling keep streets clean and cut the waste sent to landfill.
rejected.remember: Councils can lift liveability by improving spaces, paths, transport links and waste services.

a.q: Which action by a council is a strategy to improve liveability?
opts: Building a cycling path that links a suburb to the station
Closing a library to save money on staff
Removing all the bins from a local park
Cutting the number of buses on a busy route
a.why: A cycling path to the station helps people reach transport and travel safely. The other options remove services, which would usually make the place less liveable.
a.clue: Which option adds something people can use to get around?

b.q: Residents of a town in Tasmania say they cannot reach the shops without a car. Which council strategy best deals with this problem?
opts: Building footpaths and a regular bus link to the shops
Adding a second recycling bin to every home
Planting more trees in the town square
Running a weekly rubbish collection
b.why: Footpaths and a bus link help people reach the shops without a car. Recycling bins, trees and rubbish collection are useful, but they do not fix the travel problem.
b.clue: Match the strategy to the problem the residents describe.

claude_code.reason: Both versions say councils run bus and train links, but in Australia, Tasmania included, state governments run or contract trains and almost all buses. Question b's right answer in the fix also repeats 'to the shops' from the question.

a.q: A council gives every home a bin for cans and bottles and a green-waste pickup. What type of liveability strategy is this?
opts: A waste and recycling strategy
A public space strategy
A transport link strategy
A walking and cycling path strategy
a.why: Bins for cans and bottles and a green-waste pickup are recycling and rubbish services. They keep streets clean and cut waste sent to landfill. They do not create a place to meet or a way to travel, so they are not public space or transport strategies.
a.clue: Think about what happens to the cans, bottles and garden clippings.

b.q: Residents of a town in Tasmania say they cannot reach the shops without a car. Which council strategy best deals with this problem?
opts: Starting a regular bus link to the shops
Adding a second recycling bin to every home
Planting shade trees in the town square
Running a weekly rubbish collection for homes
b.why: A bus link helps people reach the shops without a car. Recycling bins, trees and rubbish collection can make a place more liveable, but they do not fix the travel problem the residents describe.
b.clue: Match the strategy to the problem the residents describe.

problems.detail: The card says local councils run many services and then lists bus or train links. In Australia, train services and most bus services are run by state or territory governments, not local councils. Brisbane City Council and a few community buses are exceptions. The card could say councils plan for or push for transport links.

In Tasmania, regular bus services are run or contracted by the state government (for example Metro Tasmania), not by local councils. Calling a new bus link a 'council strategy' in a Tasmanian town may mislead students about who provides public transport.
The right option is the only one that repeats 'to the shops' from the question stem. A student could pick it by matching words without understanding the idea.

version.title: Strategies to improve liveability
card: Liveability is how well a place meets the needs of the people who live there. Local councils can make a place more liveable in several ways.
Public spaces
building and looking after parks, playgrounds, libraries and town squares where people meet and relax.
Paths and links
building footpaths, cycling paths, bus shelters and local roads. State governments run most buses and trains, but councils can plan for, and ask for, better links.
Waste services
collecting rubbish and recycling, which keeps streets clean and sends less waste to landfill.
version.remember: Councils lift liveability through public spaces, paths and links, and waste services.

a.q: Which council action would most likely make a suburb more liveable?
opts: Building a cycling path from homes to the shops
Closing the local library to cut staff costs
Removing the rubbish bins from a busy park
Selling a park so a car park can be built
a.why: A cycling path helps people get around safely without a car. Closing a library, removing bins and selling a park all take away services or spaces that people use.
a.clue: Which action adds something people can use?

b.q: People in a small Tasmanian town say they cannot walk safely from their homes to the shops. Which council strategy fits this problem best?
opts: Build a footpath along the main street
Run a new council train line to the shops
Add a second recycling bin for each home
Plant shade trees in the town square
b.why: A footpath gives people a safe place to walk, and building footpaths is council work. A train line is tempting, but state governments run most trains, so a council would not run its own line.
b.clue: Think about what a council builds.

a.best: Building a cycling path from homes to the shops

b.best: Build a footpath along the main street

problems.detail: The three wrong options all take something away (close the library, sell a park, remove bins), and the clue asks which action adds something, so a student can pick the right answer by common sense without knowing the council strategies on the card. Wrong options that are also improvements, but less fitting or not council work, would test the idea.

check.summary: The facts and both right answers check out. Question a is too easy: every wrong option removes a service, so it can be answered without the card.
